title: Statics
tagline: Forces and moments, equilibrium of particles and rigid bodies, trusses, frames and machines, friction, centroids and moments of inertia of areas
summary: Statics is the mechanics of bodies that do not accelerate, and every bridge, crane and machine frame must first be in equilibrium. The course builds the vector tools of mechanics — forces, moments, couples and free-body diagrams — and applies the equations of equilibrium to particles, rigid bodies, trusses, frames and machines, friction, centroids and distributed loads, and the second moments of area used throughout structural design.
overview: Statics is the study of bodies that do not accelerate, and it is not an approximation to dynamics. It is the design case. Almost every artefact an engineer will ever sign for — a roof truss, a machine frame, a bracket, a foundation, a bolt group, a shelf bracket — is sized not by how it moves but by how it sits still, and the whole subject follows from two vector equations that Newton wrote down in 1687 and that Archimedes had, in effect, used for the lever two thousand years earlier: the sum of the forces is zero and the sum of the moments is zero.

The subject's real content is not the algebra but the isolation. A free-body diagram is an argument about what is touching what, and getting it wrong is not a small error but a total one: a missing reaction gives a structure that cannot stand, a spurious one gives a problem with more unknowns than equations and no way to know that the extra unknown is imaginary. The course therefore spends its first four lessons on force systems and their equivalents — resolving, reducing a system to a force and a couple, replacing a distributed load by a resultant with a stated line of action — and only then applies the equilibrium equations to a body, and then to systems of bodies, where the discipline of dismembering the system and drawing a separate diagram for each part is the difference between a solvable problem and an insoluble one.

The three great applications are treated at length. **Trusses** are frameworks of two-force members, in which the entire analysis is the observation that a member loaded at two points carries load only along the line joining them; the method of joints, the method of sections and the inspection rules for zero-force members are then arithmetic, and the arithmetic is what let nineteenth-century engineers design spans of two hundred feet with a slide rule and a drawing board. **Frames and machines** are frameworks of multi-force members, where the members bend, where the dismemberment must be chosen with care, and where the difference between a three-force member in equilibrium and a two-force member is the difference between a mechanism and a structure. **Friction** is the only irreversible force in the subject, and it is the reason a wedge holds, a belt drives, a screw lifts a tonne with one hand and a self-locking toggle stays shut when the load tries to open it.

The last two lessons build the section properties that mechanics of materials will spend a course consuming. The **centroid** is the point through which a uniform stress distribution's resultant acts, and the **second moment of area** is the quantity that decides how much a beam bends and how much stress a given bending moment produces; both are pure geometry, both are computed by the same integrals, and both are misunderstood by every student who has ever applied the parallel-axis theorem to a composite section without noticing that the theorem is about moving the axis and not about adding numbers. The course closes with **principal axes and Mohr's circle for area**, which is the first appearance in the curriculum of the idea that a quantity can depend on the orientation of the axes you measure it with — an idea that will reappear as stress, as strain, as inertia and as nothing else all the way to the end of the degree.
outcomes: Reduce an arbitrary system of forces and couples acting on a rigid body to a single resultant force and couple at a chosen point, and locate the line of action of a single-force or wrench resultant where one exists

Draw a complete free-body diagram for a particle or a rigid body in two or three dimensions, listing every applied load, reaction and couple, and state before solving whether the number of unknowns matches, exceeds or falls short of the number of independent equilibrium equations
Apply the equilibrium equations to rigid bodies in plane and space, and identify a partially constrained or improperly constrained body from the geometry of its reactions rather than from the count

Compute the moment of a force about a point and about a specified axis, use Varignon's theorem and the vector triple product interchangeably, and recognise a couple as a free vector whose moment is the same about every point

Analyse a plane truss by the method of joints and the method of sections, identify zero-force members by inspection, and classify a truss as statically determinate, statically indeterminate or a mechanism from the relation between joints, members and reactions

Dismember a frame or a machine into its members, distinguish a two-force member from a multi-force member before writing an equation, and carry the correct reaction components at each connection type — pin, roller, fixed, smooth surface, ball-and-socket

Apply Coulomb's friction laws to wedges, screws, flat and V-belts, band brakes, clutches and journal collars, compute the belt tension ratio from the capstan formula, and determine whether a machine or fastener is self-locking from the friction angle alone

Locate the centroid of a line, area or volume by integration and by the composite-body method, compute the resultant and line of action of a one-, two- or three-dimensional distributed load, and apply the theorems of Pappus to surfaces and solids of revolution

Compute the second moments of area and the product of inertia of a general section about any set of axes, apply the parallel-axis theorem correctly to a built-up section, and find the principal axes, the principal moments and the radius of gyration

Judge whether a real built-up structure should be idealised as a truss, a frame or a shell, trace the load path from the point of application to the foundation, and state which members are in tension, which in compression and which are carrying load only because the idealisation forbade them from being straight

chapters.title: Forces and vectors
chapters.summary: Force as a vector, components in two and three dimensions, resultants, and the units and dimensions of mechanics.

chapters.title: Equilibrium of a particle
chapters.summary: Free-body diagrams and the conditions for a particle to be in equilibrium in the plane and in space.

chapters.title: Moments and couples
chapters.summary: The moment of a force about a point and about an axis, couples, and equivalent force–couple systems.

chapters.title: Equilibrium of rigid bodies
chapters.summary: Supports and their reactions, the equations of equilibrium in two and three dimensions, and statical determinacy.

chapters.title: Trusses
chapters.summary: Plane trusses analysed by the method of joints and the method of sections, zero-force members and space trusses.

chapters.title: Frames and machines
chapters.summary: Multi-force members, pin forces and the analysis of frames, linkages and simple machines.

chapters.title: Friction
chapters.summary: Coulomb friction, impending slipping and tipping, wedges, screws, belts and bearings.

chapters.title: Centroids and distributed loads
chapters.summary: Centres of gravity and centroids by integration and by composite parts, and the resultants of distributed loads and fluid pressure.

chapters.title: Moments of inertia of areas
chapters.summary: Second moments of area, the parallel-axis theorem, polar and product moments, and the principal axes of cross-sections.

history.title: Stevin, the triangle of forces, and a chain over a prism
history.detail: Simon Stevin, a Flemish mathematician and engineer working in the Dutch Republic, published *De Beghinselen der Weeghconst* (statics) and *De Beghinselen des Waterwichts* (hydrostatics) at Leiden in 1586. In them he stated the law of the inclined plane, used the triangle of forces to compose and resolve forces, and computed the force of water on a submerged wall. His proof of the inclined plane is the most elegant thing in Renaissance mechanics: a closed chain draped over a triangular prism cannot set itself moving, since that would be perpetual motion, and the law of the plane follows in a few lines. **Two thousand years earlier Archimedes of Syracuse had proved the law of the lever and found the centres of gravity of plane figures; Stevin was the first to go substantially beyond him in statics.**

history.title: The Principia, and Varignon's project
history.detail: Newton's *Principia* appeared in 1687, and its corollaries on the composition of motions and forces gave the parallelogram law a dynamical foundation. In the same year Pierre Varignon published his *Projet d'une nouvelle mécanique*, which built statics on the composition of forces and stated the theorem that the moment of a resultant about a point equals the sum of the moments of its components. His fuller treatise, the *Nouvelle mécanique ou statique*, was published posthumously in 1725. **The theorem of moments is, in vector language, the distributive law of the cross product, and it is used in almost every moment calculation in this course.**

history.title: Euler, the elastic column and the indeterminate table
history.detail: Leonhard Euler's *Methodus inveniendi lineas curvas maximi minimive proprietate gaudentes* (Lausanne and Geneva, 1744) included an appendix, *De curvis elasticis*, written at Daniel Bernoulli's suggestion, which classified the shapes of the elastic curve and gave the critical load of a column; he returned to columns in his memoir *Sur la force des colonnes* of 1757. In the 1770s he took up the problem of a four-legged table resting on a rigid floor and showed that statics alone cannot divide the weight among the legs — an early explicit recognition of statical indeterminacy. **Euler's column is the first example in engineering of a structure that fails at a load far below the material's crushing strength for a reason that has nothing to do with the material: a structure's weakness is often geometric.**

history.title: Coulomb's friction
history.detail: Guillaume Amontons had reported to the Académie des Sciences in 1699 that friction is proportional to the normal load and independent of the apparent area of contact. Charles-Augustin de Coulomb's *Théorie des machines simples*, which won the Académie's prize of 1781 and was published in 1785, tested these laws over a wide range of materials, loads, contact times and speeds, distinguished static from kinetic friction, and applied the results to the friction of ropes and machines; his earlier memoir of 1773 had already applied friction to the theory of retaining walls. **That friction is independent of apparent area is a statement about asperities, and it was not until the work of Bowden and Tabor around 1950 that it was explained by the real area of contact being proportional to the load.**

history.title: The capstan formula
history.detail: Leonhard Euler derived the exponential relation between the tensions at the two ends of a rope wrapped round a post in a memoir written in 1762 and printed in Berlin in 1769, and Johann Albert Eytelwein, a Prussian hydraulic and building engineer, presented it for engineers in his *Handbuch der Statik fester Körper* (1808); it is still called the Euler–Eytelwein formula in German engineering. **It is the most counter-intuitive result in statics — with a friction coefficient of 0.3, two turns round a bollard multiply the holding force more than fortyfold — and it is why one sailor can hold a ship, why a belt drive can be light, and why a rope must not be allowed to slip round a capstan under load, because the holding power falls as soon as it slides.**

history.title: Ritter's method of sections
history.detail: August Ritter, then teaching at the polytechnic in Hanover and later professor at Aachen, published the method of sections in his *Elementare Theorie und Berechnung eiserner Dach- und Brücken-Constructionen* (1862): a truss is cut through three members and the force in each follows from a single moment equation about the intersection of the other two. It reduces the analysis of a determinate truss from a march through the joints to a few independent equations, and lets the force in any member be found directly. **The "Ritter point" — the moment centre at the intersection of two cut members — still carries his name.**

history.title: Culmann and graphical statics
history.detail: Karl Culmann published *Die Graphische Statik* at Zurich in 1866, and for decades afterwards graphical methods were the standard way of analysing bridges, roofs and cranes. The funicular and force polygons are developed there; James Clerk Maxwell's reciprocal figures of 1864, which give the forces in a plane pin-jointed truss as a single diagram, were systematised by Luigi Cremona, and Otto Mohr and Culmann's successor Wilhelm Ritter extended the graphical school. **Graphical statics was not a primitive numerical method but a genuine geometric theory: the funicular polygon is a bending-moment diagram and the reciprocal figure expresses a duality between frame and force diagram. It was displaced not by being wrong but by the calculating machine and then the computer.**
